claim: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common liver disease in industrialized countries and is increasing in prevalence.
source: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common liver disease in industrialized countries and is increasing in prevalence.
evidence: This is a statement about the epidemiology of NAFLD that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hepatocellular inhibition of Hedgehog signaling leads to steatosis by altering the abundance of the transcription factors GLI1 and GLI3.
source: Using transgenic mice with conditional hepatocyte-specific deletion of Smoothened in adult mice, we showed that hepatocellular inhibition of Hedgehog signaling leads to steatosis by altering the abundance of the transcription factors GLI1 and GLI3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic mouse models described in the manuscript.

claim: The steatotic 'Gli-code' caused the modulation of a complex network of lipogenic transcription factors and enzymes, including SREBP1 and PNPLA3.
source: This steatotic 'Gli-code' caused the modulation of a complex network of lipogenic transcription factors and enzymes, including SREBP1 and PNPLA3, as demonstrated by microarray analysis and siRNA experiments and could be confirmed in other steatotic mouse models as well as in steatotic human livers.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray analysis, siRNA experiments, and validation in multiple mouse models and human samples.

claim: Activation of the Hedgehog pathway reversed the 'Gli-code' and mitigated hepatic steatosis.
source: Conversely, activation of the Hedgehog pathway reversed the "Gli-code" and mitigated hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that pathway activation reduces steatosis.

claim: Hepatic steatosis is the hallmark feature of NAFLD.
source: Hepatic steatosis is the hallmark feature of NAFLD (Enomoto et al., 2015) and has the potential to develop into more severe steatohepatitis (NASH), which can progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis and cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enomoto et al., 2015.

claim: Steatosis occurs when the rate of fatty acid delivery exceeds the rate of fatty acid removal (oxidation and export).
source: Steatosis occurs when the rate of fatty acid delivery exceeds the rate of fatty acid removal (oxidation and export).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on established knowledge of lipid metabolism.

claim: Wnt/beta-catenin signaling was recognized as a master regulator of the zonal distribution of nitrogen metabolism in the adult liver.
source: Recently, Wnt/beta-catenin signaling was recognized as a master regulator of the zonal distribution of nitrogen metabolism in the adult liver (Benhamouche et al., 2006; Gebhardt and Hovhannisyan, 2010; Monga, 2015) and it influences the balance between the anabolic and catabolic functions of glucose metabolism (Chafey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling cascade is an important pathway that determines embryonic patterning, cell growth and tissue repair.
source: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling cascade is another important pathway that determines embryonic patterning, cell growth and tissue repair (Omenetti et al., 2011; Gu and Xie, 2015), and often acts in close crosstalk with Wnt/beta-catenin signaling (Toku et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Hh pathway can act in canonical and non-canonical manners.
source: Similar to Wnt/beta-catenin signaling, the Hh pathway can act in canonical and non-canonical manners, as explicitly described by Teperino et al. (Teperino et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Teperino et al., 2014.

claim: Active SMO triggers the activation of the GLI transcription factors by preventing the conversion of GLI2 and GLI3 into transcriptional repressors.
source: Active SMO triggers the activation of the GLI (Glioma-associated oncogene) transcription factors (TFs) (GLI1, 2 and 3) by preventing the conversion of GLI2 and GLI3 into transcriptional repressors (Ruiz i Altaba, 1999; Infante et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the canonical Hh signaling mechanism.

claim: The 'Gli-code' forms the basis of the integration of Hh signals in embryogenesis and carcinogenesis.
source: According to Ruiz I Altaba et al., the 'Gli-code', i.e. the combinatorial and cooperative function of the repressing and activating forms of all GLI factors, forms the basis of the integration of Hh signals (as well as of multiple other morphogens and cytokines) in embryogenesis and carcinogenesis (Ruiz i Altaba, 1999; Ruiz i Altaba et al., 2003; 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ruiz i Altaba's work defining the Gli-code concept.

claim: Hh signaling plays a considerable role in various scenarios of adult liver regeneration from progenitor cells.
source: To date, Hh signaling has been found to play a considerable role in various scenarios of adult liver regeneration from progenitor cells (Sicklick et al., 2006) and in the regulation of the compensatory outgrowth of progenitors and myofibroblasts (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The regulation of the IGF-axis in mature hepatocytes is controlled by Hh signaling.
source: Regarding liver metabolism, we recently showed that the regulation of the IGF-axis (insulin-like growth factor) in mature hepatocytes is controlled by Hh signaling (Matz-Soja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The TFs GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3 form a unique self-stabilizing network in hepatocytes and regulate several metabolic genes, including lipid associated factors.
source: Moreover, we were also able to show that the TFs GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3 form a unique self-stabilizing network in hepatocytes and regulate several metabolic genes, including lipid associated factors (Schmidt-Heck et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Triple transgenic mice with conditional hepatocyte-specific ablation of Smo in response to doxycycline were generated.
source: As depicted in Figure 1A–B, triple transgenic mice which have a conditional hepatocyte-specific ablation of Smo in response to doxycycline (abbreviated SLC mice) were generated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description in the text and Figure 1A-B showing the breeding scheme.

claim: The Smotm2Amc/J mice possess loxP sites flanking exon 1 of the Smo gene.
source: Thus, the Smotm2Amc/J mice (Jackson Laboratories), which possess loxP sites flanking exon 1 of the Smo gene (Long et al., 2001), were crossed with the LC-1/rTALAP-1 mice which are working with a tetracycline-controlled transcriptional activation of the Cre recombinase protein (provided by Hermann Bujard) (Schonig et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Long et al., 2001.

claim: Hepatocyte-specific ablation of Smo was induced at the age of 8 weeks to avoid the hormonal complications of adolescence.
source: At the age of 8 weeks (to avoid the hormonal complications of adolescence), hepatocyte-specific ablation of Smo was induced by adding 2 mg/ml doxycycline hydrochloride (Sigma, Germany) to the drinking water for 10 days to promote the expression of the Cre recombinase (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental protocol described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After 10 days of doxycycline treatment, nearly all hepatocytes were positive for Cre recombinase protein.
source: After 10 days, nearly all hepatocytes were positive for Cre recombinase protein (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was a significant decrease in Smo expression in the liver material and isolated hepatocytes after sacrifice.
source: After sacrifice, the specificity of the Smo deletion was measured via qRT-PCR, indicating that there was a significant decrease in Smo expression in the liver material and isolated hepatocytes (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No adverse side effect of the doxycycline treatment could be observed on body weight.
source: As already shown in our previous article, no adverse side effect of the doxycycline treatment could be observed on body weight (Matz-Soja et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The expression of important genes of lipid metabolism in hepatocytes was not affected by doxycycline.
source: Likewise, the expression of important genes of lipid metabolism in hepatocytes was not affected by doxycycline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The deletion of Smo at 8 weeks of age resulted in pronounced liver steatosis within 5 weeks.
source: The deletion of Smo at 8 weeks of age resulted in pronounced liver steatosis within 5 weeks (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The H&E and fat red staining clearly showed lipid droplet accumulations, which are most prominent in the midzone to periportal zone.
source: The H&E and fat red staining clearly showed lipid droplet accumulations, which are most prominent in the midzone to periportal zone, but occasionally encompassed the entire parenchyma (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological staining shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Quantification of the fat red staining revealed a 7-fold increase in the SLC-KO mice compared with the WT controls.
source: Quantification of the fat red staining revealed a 7-fold increase in the SLC-KO mice compared with the WT controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Insulin resistance does not contribute to the steatosis in SLC-KO mice at least during the first five weeks after doxycycline administration.
source: Because the insulin and glucose levels changed only marginally (Table 1), we conclude that insulin resistance does not contribute to the steatosis in SLC-KO mice at least during the first five weeks after doxycycline administration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the insulin and glucose measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: No significant changes in hepatic expression for insulin receptor (Insr), insulin receptor substrate 1 and 2 (Irs1/2) could be detected.
source: This assumption is confirmed by the fact that we could not detect any significant changes in hepatic expression for insulin receptor (Insr), insulin receptor substrate 1 and 2 (Irs1/2) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no other indications of overt liver damage in the SLC-KO mice with the exception of the steatosis and lower liver/body weight ratio.
source: With the exception of the steatosis and lower liver/body weight ratio compared with the SLC-WT mice (Figure 2C), there were no other indications of overt liver damage in the SLC-KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the liver/body weight ratio data shown in Figure 2C and the absence of other damage markers.

claim: The serum activities of ASAT, ALAT and GLDH were not different from those of the SLC-WT mice.
source: Accordingly, the serum activities of ASAT (aspartate aminotransferase), ALAT (alanine aminotransferase) and GLDH (glutamate dehydrogenase) were not different from those of the SLC-WT mice (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by serum enzyme activity measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The plasma triglyceride levels were significantly increased in the VLDL fraction, while no changes were found in LDL and HDL fractions.
source: The plasma triglyceride levels were significantly increased in the VLDL (very low density lipoprotein) fraction, while no changes were found in LDL (low density lipoprotein) and HDL (high density lipoprotein) fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipoprotein measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Steatosis is not caused by an impairment of triglyceride secretion from the hepatocytes.
source: These findings indicate that steatosis is not caused by an impairment of triglyceride secretion from the hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VLDL triglycerides are increased, suggesting secretion is not impaired.

claim: The inhibition of Hh signaling in cultured mouse and human hepatocytes using the SMO inhibitor cyclopamine resulted in marked steatosis within 48 to 72 hr.
source: In addition to these results in vivo, the inhibition of Hh signaling in cultured mouse and human hepatocytes using the SMO inhibitor cyclopamine (Hovhannisyan et al., 2009) also resulted in marked steatosis within 48 to 72 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ihh and Shh were down-regulated in SLC-KO hepatocytes, consistent with a decrease in pathway activity due to the deletion of Smo.
source: Regarding Hh ligands, we could observe a down-regulation of Ihh and Shh, consistent with a decrease in pathway activity due to the deletion of Smo (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ihh is the most abundantly expressed ligand in hepatocytes, whereas Shh is hard to detect and Dhh was not measureable.
source: It is worth noting that Ihh is the most abundantly expressed ligand in hepatocytes, whereas Shh is hard to detect and Dhh was not measureable.
evidence: This claim is based on the expression measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: No significant changes in the Ptch1, Ptch2 and Hhip transcripts were observed in SLC-KO mice.
source: Regarding the receptors, we did not observe significant changes in the Ptch1, Ptch2 and Hhip (Hedgehog-interacting protein) transcripts, which was also true for Fu (Fused) and Sufu (Suppressor of fused) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The Gli1 and Gli3 mRNAs were significantly decreased in the SLC-KO mice, while the Gli2 mRNA remained unchanged.
source: However, the Gli1 and Gli3 mRNAs were significantly decreased in the SLC-KO mice, while the Gli2 mRNA remained unchanged (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GLI1 and GLI3 are well detectable in hepatocyte nuclei in SLC-WT mice, but are absent in nuclei of SLC-KO hepatocytes.
source: The results clearly demonstrate that GLI1 and GLI3, are well detectable in hepatocyte nuclei in SLC-WT mice, but are absent in nuclei of SLC-KO hepatocytes (white arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: In SLC-KO livers, GLI1 and GLI3 are only present in non-parenchymal cells, e.g. bile duct epithelial cells.
source: In SLC-KO livers, these TFs are only present in non-parenchymal cells, e.g. bile duct epithelial cells (Figure 3E,F, yellow arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The amount of GLI3/A (full length activator protein) was significantly reduced in SLC-KO hepatocytes.
source: The results clearly show that the amount of GLI3/A (full length activator protein) was significantly reduced in SLC-KO hepatocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: In melanocortin-4-receptor-deficient mice (MC4R) and Lepob/ob mice, the expression of Gli1 and Gli3 was obviously reduced, whereas Gli2 expression either did not change (MC4R-KO mice) or was increased (ob/ob mice).
source: In both mouse models, the expression of Gli1 and Gli3 was obviously reduced, whereas Gli2 expression either did not change (MC4R-KO mice) or was increased (ob/ob mice) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from MC4R-KO and ob/ob mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The same transcriptional changes of the Gli factors were detected in human patients with clinical relevant steatosis compared to non-steatotic patients.
source: Furthermore we could detect the same transcriptional changes of the Gli factors in human patients with clinical relevant steatosis compared to non-steatotic patients (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from human liver samples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: At a cut-off level of 1.5-fold, 179 genes were up-regulated in Chip Arrays and 106 genes were down-regulated.
source: At a cut-off level of 1.5-fold, 179 genes were up-regulated in Chip Arrays and 106 genes were down-regulated.
evidence: This claim is based on microarray analysis data.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using ClueGO revealed highly significant changes in a number of metabolic functions, particularly those involved in lipid metabolism.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using ClueGO revealed highly significant changes in a number of metabolic functions, particularly those involved in lipid metabolism (Figure 4A) (Figure 4—source data 1—data).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The GO term 'lipid metabolic process' showed pronounced up-regulation of 30 genes with a p-value of 7.70E-11.
source: For instance, the GO term 'lipid metabolic process' showed pronounced up-regulation of 30 genes (p-value of 7.70E-11) many of which (e.g. Ppara, Pparg, Srebf1, Aacs, Elovl6 and Fas) were verified by qRT-PCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis and qRT-PCR validation.

claim: Many regulated genes in the SLC-KO mice belong to the top 50 ones described to be mostly correlated with elevated hepatic triglyceride level among 100 unique inbred mouse strains.
source: In addition, the GSEA revealed that many regulated genes in the SLC-KO mice (e.g. Cd36, Avpr1a, Ttc23, Lifr andFabp2) belong to the top 50 ones described to be mostly correlated with elevated hepatic triglyceride level among 100 unique inbred mouse strains (Hui et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis and a citation to Hui et al., 2015.

claim: The GO term 'metabolic process' showed pronounced up-regulation of 113 genes reaching a p-value of 1.24E-9.
source: The GO term 'metabolic process' showed pronounced up-regulation of 113 genes reaching a p-value of 1.24E-9 indicating that genes from other metabolic processes also responded to the Smo knockout.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis.

claim: The significant up-regulation of several TFs involved in the regulation of lipid and carbohydrate metabolism was detected including Chrebp, Srebf1, Srebf2, Ppara and Pparg in SLC-KO mice.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, the significant up-regulation of several TFs involved in the regulation of lipid and carbohydrate metabolism was detected including Chrebp (Carbohydrate-responsive element-binding protein), Srebf1, Srebf2 (Sterol regulatory element binding transcription factor 1/2), Ppara and Pparg (Peroxisome proliferator activated receptor alpha/gamma) in SLC-KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The SREBP1 protein showed a slightly pericentral and rare nuclear preference in liver parenchyma from SLC-WT mice and was very strongly enhanced in the pericentral zone of livers from SLC-KO mice.
source: The SREBP1 protein showed a slightly pericentral and rare nuclear preference in liver parenchyma from SLC-WT mice and was very strongly enhanced in the pericentral zone of livers from SLC-KO mice. In particular, the frequency of nuclear staining in hepatocytes was much higher in these mice compared to control mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PPARG protein was much more frequent in hepatocyte nuclei of SLC-KO mice than in SLC-WT mice.
source: Likewise, PPARG protein was much more frequent in hepatocyte nuclei of SLC-KO mice than in SLC-WT mice. Also with PPARG heterogeneous distribution of the protein was obvious (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The gene expression of the anti-adipogenic TF Gata4 was significantly reduced, whereas Gata6 remained unchanged.
source: Additionally, the gene expression of the anti-adipogenic TF Gata4 (Patankar et al., 2012) was significantly reduced, whereas Gata6 remained unchanged (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Patankar et al., 2012.

claim: The Nfyb mRNA was markedly reduced, while the Nfyg and Lxra mRNAs remained unaffected.
source: The Nfyb (Nuclear transcription factor-Y beta) mRNA was also markedly reduced, while the Nfyg (Nuclear transcription factor-Y gamma) and Lxra (Liver X receptor alpha) mRNAs remained unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression measurements.

claim: The expression of Foxa1 and Foxa2, which are known to mediate the effects of insulin on lipid metabolism, did not change.
source: The expression of Foxa1 and Foxa2 (Forkhead box A1/2), which are known to mediate the effects of insulin on lipid metabolism (Wolfrum et al., 2004), did not change (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Wolfrum et al., 2004.

claim: The expression of Nr1d2 was strongly down-regulated, while that of Nr1d1 remained unchanged.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Nr1d2 (Rev-ErbA beta) was strongly down-regulated, while that of Nr1d1 (Rev-ErbA alpha) remained unchanged (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increased expression of enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of fatty acids and triglycerides was found, including Acaca, Fasn, Elovl6 and Gpam.
source: Of the key lipogenic enzymes, we found increased expression of those involved in the biosynthesis of fatty acids and triglycerides, including Acaca (Acetyl-Coenzyme A carboxylase alpha), Fasn (fatty acid synthase), Elovl6 (Elongation of long chain fatty acids) and Gpam (Glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The expression of Acacb was not changed, and Elovl3 expression was significantly decreased.
source: In contrast, the expression of Acacb was not changed, and Elovl3 expression was significantly decreased (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The transcripts for enzymes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, such as Aacs, Hmgcr, and Lss, were increased.
source: The transcripts for enzymes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, such as Aacs (acetoacetyl-CoA synthetase), Hmgcr (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-Coenzyme A reductase), and Lss (Lanosterol synthase), were also increased (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The NAFLD-associated gene Pnpla3 was dramatically increased.
source: Intriguingly, the newly discovered NAFLD-associated gene Pnpla3 (Adiponutrin) (Chow et al., 2014; Smagris et al., 2015) was also dramatically increased (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D and citations to Chow et al., 2014 and Smagris et al., 2015.

claim: The stronger staining of FASN confirmed the up-regulation of FASN in the SLC-KO mice and revealed a shift from the known pericentral to the periportal localization in the SLC-WT mice.
source: The stronger staining not only confirmed the up-regulation of FASN in the SLC-KO mice, but, surprisingly, revealed a shift from the known pericentral (Gebhardt, 1992; Postic and Girard, 2008) to the periportal localization in the SLC-WT mice, matching the preferential site of lipid accumulation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 6A and citations to Gebhardt, 1992 and Postic and Girard, 2008.

claim: Hh signaling is required to maintain the normal zonation of the liver parenchyma, at least with respect to lipid metabolism.
source: These results suggest that in addition to Wnt/beta-catenin signaling (Benhamouche et al., 2006; Gebhardt and Hovhannisyan, 2010), Hh signaling is required to maintain the normal zonation of the liver parenchyma, at least with respect to lipid metabolism.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in FASN zonation and supported by citations.

claim: Fatty acid biosynthesis, as determined by the incorporation of [14C]-labelled acetate, was almost doubled in the hepatocytes from the SLC-KO mice.
source: Fatty acid biosynthesis, as determined by the incorporation of [14C]-labelled acetate, was almost doubled in the hepatocytes from the SLC-KO mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cholesterol biosynthesis from labelled acetate was not changed in vitro.
source: However, cholesterol biosynthesis from labelled acetate was not changed in vitro (Figure 6B), corresponding to the unchanged serum cholesterol levels in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic assay data shown in Figure 6B and serum cholesterol data.

claim: The hepatocytes from the SLC-KO mice showed a significantly higher rate of fatty acid synthesis from [14C(U)]-glucose in the presence of 10 mM glucose and 0.1 µM insulin.
source: Interestingly, the hepatocytes from the SLC-KO mice showed a significantly higher rate of fatty acid synthesis from [14C(U)]-glucose in the presence of 10 mM glucose and 0.1 µM insulin (Figure 6C), suggesting increased channeling of the high concentrations of glucose into fatty acid biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Neither the glycogen content, nor basal or stimulated glycolysis as determined by the conversion of [14C(U)]-glucose to lactate were altered in the hepatocytes from the re-fed SLC-KO mice.
source: The fact that neither the glycogen content (Figure 6D), nor basal or stimulated glycolysis as determined by the conversion of [14C(U)]-glucose to lactate (Figure 6E) were altered in the hepatocytes from the re-fed SLC-KO mice, suggests that there is no shortage of potential fuel for glycolytic acetyl-CoA formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic assay data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Electron microscopy revealed larger and swollen mitochondria in the SLC-KO mice.
source: Electron microscopy revealed larger and swollen mitochondria in the SLC-KO mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 6F.

claim: ATP levels were significantly reduced in SLC-KO hepatocytes.
source: Further analyses showed significantly reduced ATP levels (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The activity of the respiratory complexes was not changed.
source: However, the activity of the respiratory complexes was not changed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of carrier proteins (e.g. Cpt1a, Cpt2) and enzymes (Acox1, Acadvl) of beta oxidation were not changed.
source: The expression of carrier proteins (e.g. Cpt1a, Cpt2; Carnitine palmitoyltransferases 1a/2) and enzymes (Acox1, acyl-Coenzyme A oxidase 1, and Acadvl, acyl-Coenzyme A dehydrogenase, very long chain) of beta oxidation were also not changed (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: A significant decrease of Slc25a5 expression was found, which transports ADP and ATP through the mitochondrial inner membrane.
source: Instead, we found the significant decrease of Slc25a5 (mitochondrial carrier) expression, which transports ADP and ATP through the mitochondrial inner membrane (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: No significant changes in the ketone body concentrations could be measured.
source: The fact that no significant changes in the ketone body concentrations could be measured (Figure 6J), lead us to speculate that the decrease of SLC25a5 could be one explanation of the low ATP production.
evidence: This claim is supported by ketone body measurements shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Gli3 knockdown led to a significant increase in the expression of lipogenic TFs including Ppara, Pparg, and Srebf1.
source: Gli3 knockdown led to a significant increase in the expression of lipogenic TFs including Ppara, Pparg, and Srebf1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Only the hepatocytes treated with Gli3 siRNA responded with an increase in the expression of Fasn and Elovl6 and a reduced expression of Elovl3.
source: Likewise, only the hepatocytes treated with Gli3 siRNA responded with an increase in the expression of Fasn and Elovl6 and a reduced expression of Elovl3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mainly the hepatocytes transfected with the Gli3 siRNA showed pronounced accumulation of fat droplets and elevated lipid staining after 72 hr.
source: To validate the transcriptional data we focused on the lipid content of siRNA-treated cultures. Mainly the hepatocytes transfected with the Gli3 siRNA showed pronounced accumulation of fat droplets (Figure 7B) and elevated lipid staining after 72 hr (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fat red staining data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Gli1 knockdown may aid in inducing steatosis to a minor extent, because Srebf1 was also induced under this condition.
source: To a minor extent Gli1 knockdown may aid in inducing steatosis, because Srebf1 was also induced under this condition (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Srebf1 is induced by Gli1 knockdown.

claim: Chrebp expression did not change in Gli knockdown experiments, suggesting that the up-regulation observed in the SLC-KO mice is either due to a GLI-independent mechanism or reflects another adaptive response in vivo.
source: Chrebp expression did not change in these experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the up-regulation observed in the SLC-KO mice (Figure 4B) is either due to a GLI-independent mechanism or reflects another adaptive response in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of Chrebp response to Gli knockdown.

claim: ChIP experiments provided first hints for a direct regulation of Srebf1 gene expression via binding sites for the GLI3 protein in its promotor region.
source: Using data mining by MotivMap analyses (Daily et al., 2011) several possible binding sites for the GLI3 protein within the range of − 10000 bp upstream to 10000 bp downstream of the transcription start site of the Fasn, Ppara and Srebf1 genes were identified. As consensus sequence we selected TGTGTGGTC for the ChIP analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A). The data provided in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B give a first hint that direct binding of GLI3 to the predicted binding site in the promoter region of Srebf1 (at -1156 bp) might be involved in transmitting GLI factor activity to the expression of SREBP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and MotivMap analysis.

claim: No hint was found that GLI3 directly binds to Fasn and Ppara promoters, making it more likely that these proteins are not primary, but secondary targets of GLI3.
source: No such hint was found, however, in the case of Fasn (at the predicted binding site at -1767 bp) and Ppara (at the predicted binding site at -2674 bp) making it more likely that these proteins are not primary, but secondary targets of GLI3 (mediated among else by SREBP1, see below).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of ChIP evidence for direct GLI3 binding to Fasn and Ppara promoters.

claim: Sufu siRNA significantly reduced Sufu mRNA levels and strongly up-regulated expression of all Gli TFs in hepatocytes from C57BL6/N mice.
source: Ad (i), Sufu siRNA significantly reduced Sufu mRNA levels (Figure 8A) and strongly up-regulatedexpression of all Gli TFs (Figure 8B) in hepatocytes from C57BL6/N mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: A significant decrease of Srebf1 and a slight down-regulation of Srebf2 and Elovl6 were detected in Sufu knockdown cells.
source: Regarding the lipogenic TFs, a significant decrease of Srebf1 and a slight down-regulation of Srebf2 and Elovl6 were detected in the treated cells (Figure 8C) indicating that up-regulation of the Gli TFs, i. e. reversal of the steatotic GLI code, causes anti-steatotic modulation of lipogenic genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Sufu knockdown reduced hepatic steatosis in isolated hepatocytes from MC4R-KO mice.
source: Using isolated hepatocytes from MC4R-KO mice, which retain their steatotic phenotype in vitro, we demonstrated a loss of staining intensity in the cultures treated with the Sufu siRNA compared with the cultures transfected with the control (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fat red staining data shown in Figure 8D,E.

claim: A significant reduction in fat red staining was observed when the steatotic hepatocytes from the MC4R-KO and ob/ob mice were incubated with the SMO agonist SAG and recombinant SHH.
source: Ad (ii), We also could observed a significant reduction in fat red staining when the steatotic hepatocytes from the MC4R-KO and ob/ob mice were incubated with the SMO agonist SAG and recombinant SHH (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fat red staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The transfection of the GLI plasmids leads to a strong increase in the corresponding Gli mRNA expression.
source: The results clearly show that the transfection of the GLI plasmids leads to a strong increase in the corresponding Gli mRNA expression, while the combined transfection of GLI1 and GLI3 expression plasmids resulted in a slightly lower expression of the corresponding Gli mRNAs (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 9A-C.

claim: Overexpression of one Gli factor alone is not able to reduce the lipid content, but the combination of GLI1 and GLI3 significantly mitigated the steatosis in the hepatocytes from ob/ob mice.
source: The results from quantitative and qualitative analysis of fat red staining indicate that overexpression of one Gli factor alone is not able to reduce the lipid content. However, the combination of GLI1 and GLI3 significantly mitigated the steatosis in the hepatocytes from ob/ob mice (Figure 9D,E) indicating that parallel changes in both GLI factors are required to reverse steatosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by fat red staining data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 9D,E.

claim: The hepatocyte-specific impairment of canonical Hh signaling by the conditional ablation of Smo results in considerable changes in liver lipid metabolism that ultimately lead to hepatic steatosis.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that the hepatocyte-specific impairment of canonical Hh signaling by the conditional ablation of Smo results in considerable changes in liver lipid metabolism that ultimately lead to hepatic steatosis.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the entire body of experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The undisturbed Hh pathway is necessary to maintain the proper balance between the synthesis/uptake and degradation/export of fatty acids and triglycerides in adult hepatocytes.
source: Hence, the undisturbed Hh pathway is necessary to maintain the proper balance between the synthesis/uptake and degradation/export of fatty acids and triglycerides in adult hepatocytes (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is a summary claim inferred from the experimental results and illustrated in Figure 10A.

claim: A large set of lipogenic TFs and enzymes were significantly up-regulated following the deletion of Smo.
source: On the transcriptional level, we showed that a large set of lipogenic TFs and enzymes were significantly up-regulated following the deletion of Smo.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Srebf1, Ppara and Pparg were strongly increased, which are characteristic for liver steatosis.
source: Among the responding TFs were Srebf1, Ppara and Pparg strongly increased which are characteristic for liver steatosis (Fabbrini et al., 2010; Ables, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to Fabbrini et al., 2010 and Ables, 2012.

claim: Combinatorial interactions between Srepf1, Nfyb and Nfyg, and Sp1 have been shown to determine the expression of specific sets of target genes, including hundreds of genes with distinct roles in lipid metabolism.
source: Interestingly, combinatorial interactions between Srepf1, Nfyb and Nfyg (Nuclear transcription factor Y), and Sp1 (Transacting transcription factor 1) have been shown to determine the expression of specific sets of target genes, including hundreds of genes with distinct roles in lipid metabolism and other functions (Reed et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reed et al., 2008.

claim: The differential response of Nr1d1 and Nr1d2 may indicate that Hh signaling in hepatocytes could also influence the circadian fluctuations of lipid metabolism.
source: Likewise, the differential response of Nr1d1 and Nr1d2, which relate the circadian rhythm to metabolism and disease (Duez and Staels, 2008; Ramanathan et al., 2014), may indicate that Hh signaling in hepatocytes could also influence the circadian fluctuations of lipid metabolism.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the differential expression of Nr1d1 and Nr1d2 and supported by citations.

claim: Increased Acaca but not Acacb expression and increased Elovl6 expression, particularly when coupled to the down-regulation of Elovl3, should trigger lipogenesis.
source: For instance, increased Acaca but not Acacb expression (Chow et al., 2014) and increased Elovl6 expression, particularly when coupled to the down-regulation of Elovl3, should trigger lipogenesis (Jakobsson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression patterns and supported by citations to Chow et al., 2014 and Jakobsson et al., 2005.

claim: Pnpla3 has frequently been found to be associated with steatosis where it acts as a downstream gene of SREBP-1c to promote lipid accumulation.
source: Intriguingly, one of these changes concerned the increased expression of Pnpla3 which has frequently been found to be associated with steatosis where it acts as a downstream gene of SREBP-1c to promote lipid accumulation (Smagris et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smagris et al., 2015.

claim: Hh signaling may also influence carbohydrate metabolism in the presence of excess glucose, possibly by increasing Chrebp expression.
source: Thus, Hh signaling may also influence carbohydrate metabolism in the presence of excess glucose, possibly by increasing Chrebp expression.
evidence: This is a speculative claim inferred from the observation of increased liponeogenesis with high glucose.

claim: The Hh pathway appears to play an important role in liver zonation, which is shown by the completely changed zonation of FASN in response to the loss of Smo.
source: Another important result of our investigation is that the Hh pathway appears to play an important role in liver zonation, which is shown by the completely changed zonation of FASN in response to the loss of Smo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed changes in FASN zonation.

claim: The strong enhancement of SREBP1 und PPRAG protein expression in the SLC-KO mice occurred in the pericentral zone which is in line with published data from mice fed with a high fat diet.
source: Most importantly, the strong enhancement of SREBP1 und PPRAG protein expression in the SLC-KO mice occurred in the pericentral zone which is in line with published data from mice fed with a high fat diet (Inoue et al., 2005; Liu, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data and citations to Inoue et al., 2005 and Liu, 2012.

claim: SREBP1 has binding sites at -7000 bp and -500 bp of the Fasn gene.
source: For SREBP1 it was shown that this protein has binding sites at -7000 bp and -500 bp of the Fasn gene (Amemiya-Kudo et al., 2002; Morishita et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amemiya-Kudo et al., 2002 and Morishita et al., 2014.

claim: Overexpression of SREBP1c, an isoform of SREBP1, lead to significant upregulation of Fasn gene expression in hepatocytes.
source: Furthermore it was also shown that overexpression of SREBP1c, an isoform of SREBP1, lead to significant upregulation of Fasn gene expression in hepatocytes (Dentin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dentin et al., 2004.

claim: A specific transcriptional signature within the Gli TF network termed the 'steatotic Gli-code' leads to the observed steatosis in vivo and in vitro.
source: This indicates that a specific transcriptional signature within the Gli TF network which can be termed the 'steatotic Gli-code' lead to the observed steatosis in vivo and in vitro.This signature is characterized by reduced expression of Gli1 and Gli3, while Gli2 is unchanged (or slightly increased), which can be abbreviated as Gli1/Gli2/Gli3.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim inferred from the pattern of Gli factor expression changes.

claim: The postulated 'steatotic Gli-code' is universal across several strains and species promoting lipid accumulation in hepatocytes regardless of the manner of the etiology of steatosis.
source: Using different mouse models with strong steatosis by hyperphagy or leptin deficiency (e.g. MC4R and ob/ob mice), we observed the same direction of the regulation of the Gli TF's. This was also supported by measurements of Gli expression in liver samples from human patients with steatosis. These results indicate that the postulated "steatotic Gli-code" is universal across several strains and species promoting lipid accumulation in hepatocytes regardless of the manner of the etiology of steatosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from multiple mouse models and human samples.

claim: The GLI proteins are regulated by other signaling pathways, e.g. EGFR-MEK/ERK, RAS/AKT, TGF-beta and Wnt/beta-catenin signaling.
source: Because the GLI proteins are also regulated by other signaling pathways, e.g. EGFR-MEK/ERK, RAS/AKT, TGF-beta and Wnt/beta-catenin signaling (for review see [Fernandez-Zapico, 2008]), the 'Gli-code' may reflect the outcome of integrating different signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fernandez-Zapico, 2008.

claim: Similar changes in the expression of the Gli factors were found during adipogenic induction of 3T3-L1 fibroblasts.
source: Regarding lipid metabolic processes, Suh and co-workers found similar changes in the expression of the Gli factors during adipogenic induction of 3T3-L1 fibroblasts (Suh et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suh et al., 2006.

claim: The transition from the normal GLI-code (GLI1/GLI2/GLI3) to the postulated 'steatotic Gli-code' (GLI1/GLI2/GLI3) provides a novel paradigm for the regulation of lipid metabolism in the liver.
source: These similarities lead us to hypothesize that the transition from the normal GLI-code (GLI1/GLI2/GLI3) to the postulated 'steatotic Gli-code' (GLI1/GLI2/GLI3) provides a novel paradigm for the regulation of lipid metabolism in the liver (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a conceptual claim that synthesizes the experimental findings into a paradigm, illustrated in Figure 10B.

claim: The combined overexpression of GLI1 and GLI3 (but not of each GLI factor alone) is able to significantly lower the lipid content of hepatocytes from steatotic ob/ob mice.
source: This concept is considerably supported by the finding that the combined overexpression of GLI1 and GLI3 (but not of each GLI factor alone) is able to significantly lower the lipid content of hepatocytes from steatotic ob/ob mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by overexpression experiments showing that combined GLI1 and GLI3 overexpression reduces steatosis.

claim: Work by Gurdziel and coworkers supports our findings by identifying a comprehensive library of enriched GLI binding motifs in which the promotor regions of Srebf1 and Pnpla3 are predicted to harbor Hh activity via GLI binding sites.
source: Importantly, work by Gurdziel and coworkers (Gurdziel et al., 2016) published during revision of our manuscript supports our findings by identifying a comprehensive library of enriched GLI binding motifs in which among else the promotor regions of Srebf1 and Pnpla3 are predicted to harbor Hh activity via GLI binding sites (Gurdziel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gurdziel et al., 2016.

claim: The down-regulation of IGF1 observed in the SLC-KO mice may cause indirect alterations in the transcriptome in the liver and in other organs.
source: Even the down-regulation of IGF1 which we observed in the SLC-KO mice and the closely related SAC mice (Matz-Soja et al., 2014) may cause indirect alterations in the transcriptome in the liver and in other organs.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential indirect effects, supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The relevance of our findings for the human liver is emphasized by the observation that increased lipid droplets occur in human hepatocytes when the Hh pathway was inhibited by cyclopamine.
source: The relevance of our findings for the human liver is emphasized by our observation that increased lipid droplets occur in human hepatocytes when the Hh pathway was inhibited by cyclopamine.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experiments with human hepatocytes.

claim: The obvious down-regulation of Gli1 and Gli3 in human livers with steatosis supports the universality of the postulated 'steatotic Gli-code'.
source: Furthermore, the obvious down-regulation of Gli1 and Gli3 in human livers with steatosis supports the universality of the postulated 'steatotic Gli-code' and reveals new insights in the regulation of hepatic lipid metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from human liver samples.

claim: The strong up-regulation of Pnpla3 correlates with the expression changes observed in human NAFLD.
source: In addition, the strong up-regulation of Pnpla3 also correlates with the expression changes observed in human NAFLD (Romeo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Romeo et al., 2008.

claim: The dramatic down-regulation of hepatic Igf1 expression and the upregulation of Igfbp1 were observed in several clinical studies and are strongly associated with NAFLD and the metabolic syndrome.
source: Both, the dramatic down-regulation of hepatic Igf1 expression and the upregulation of Igfbp1, which were reflected in changes of the serum levels of these proteins, were observed in several clinical studies and are strongly associated with NAFLD and the metabolic syndrome (Völzke et al., 2009; Alderete et al., 2011; Mallea-Gil et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Activation of Hh signaling via the Sufu siRNA, recombinant SHH, the Hh agonist SAG and the combined overexpression of GLI1 and GLI3 was able to significantly reduce the expression of Srebf1 and mitigate the accumulation of lipids in steatotic hepatocytes.
source: The central role of the Hh signaling pathway in liver steatosis is emphasized by our findings in vitro that activation of Hh signaling via the Sufu siRNA, recombinant SHH, the Hh agonist SAG and the combined overexpression of GLI1 and GLI3 was able to significantly reduce the expression of Srebf1 and mitigate the accumulation of lipids in steatotic hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple in vitro experiments showing that pathway activation reduces steatosis.

claim: High over-activation of Hh signaling may enhance the risk for carcinogenesis.
source: However, a limiting factor may be that high over-activation of Hh signaling may enhance the risk for carcinogenesis .
evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on established knowledge about Hh signaling and cancer.

claim: The potential of impaired Hh signaling to trigger steatosis independent of nutritional changes suggests that malfunctions in this pathway may pave the way for the development of NAFLD long before other cues may lead to further aggravation.
source: The potential of impaired Hh signaling to trigger steatosis independent of nutritional changes suggests that malfunctions in this pathway may pave the way for the development of NAFLD long before other cues may lead to further aggravation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the clinical implications of the findings.
